title: Mistretta v. United States (1989)
shortTitle: Mistretta v. United States (1989) — assigned accounts
summary: Congress may delegate the writing of binding sentencing guidelines to an expert commission located in the Judicial Branch, because the statute supplies an intelligible principle and the arrangement does not undermine any branch.
notes:
Key line: Applying this intelligible principle test to congressional delegations, our jurisprudence has been driven by a practical understanding that in our increasingly complex society, replete with ever changing and more technical problems, Congress simply cannot do its job absent an ability to delegate power under broad general directives. (Justice Blackmun)

Citation: 488 U.S. 361 (1989).

sections.Parties: The petitioner in No. 87-7028 was John Mistretta, who had been indicted in the United States District Court for the Western District of Missouri on three counts arising from a cocaine sale. The respondent was the United States, which was also the petitioner in the cross-petition No. 87-1904. Alan B. Morrison argued for Mistretta and Solicitor General Charles Fried for the Government. The United States Sentencing Commission, whose guidelines were at issue, appeared as amicus curiae through Paul M. Bator. Both Houses of Congress also filed amicus briefs supporting the guidelines.
sections.Material Facts: Congress passed the Sentencing Reform Act of 1984 to replace indeterminate sentencing and parole, which had produced wide disparities and uncertainty about release dates. The Act created the United States Sentencing Commission as an independent commission in the Judicial Branch with seven voting members appointed by the President with Senate consent, at least three of them federal judges chosen from a list of six recommended by the Judicial Conference, removable by the President only for cause. The Commission was to promulgate binding guidelines setting ranges of determinate sentences for categories of offenses and offenders, guided by detailed statutory directions on the purposes of sentencing, offense and offender characteristics and the permitted width of each range. Mistretta pleaded guilty to conspiracy to distribute cocaine and was sentenced under the guidelines to eighteen months of imprisonment and other penalties. He argued the Commission was unconstitutionally constituted and had been given excessive legislative power.
sections.Procedural History: Mistretta moved in the District Court to have the guidelines declared unconstitutional. The court upheld them, 682 F. Supp. 1033 (1988), and sentenced him under them. He filed a notice of appeal to the Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit, but both he and the United States petitioned for certiorari before judgment under the Court's Rule 18 because of the disarray among district courts on the question. The Supreme Court granted both petitions, heard argument on October 5, 1988, and decided the cases on January 18, 1989, affirming by a vote of eight to one. Justice Blackmun wrote for the Court; Justice Brennan joined all but footnote 11.
sections.Issue: Did the Sentencing Reform Act delegate legislative power to the Sentencing Commission without an intelligible principle sufficient to satisfy the nondelegation doctrine? Did Congress violate the separation of powers by placing the Commission within the Judicial Branch, by requiring federal judges to serve on it alongside nonjudges and to share in writing binding policy, and by giving the President power to appoint the members and to remove them for cause, thereby threatening the independence of the Judiciary or expanding its powers beyond adjudication?
sections.Holding: The guidelines are constitutional. The Act does not delegate excessive legislative power: it specifies the goals of sentencing, the tools the Commission must use and detailed factors it must consider, which is more than the intelligible principle that Hampton, Yakus and later cases require. Placing the Commission in the Judicial Branch does not violate the separation of powers, because Congress may call on the accumulated wisdom of the Judiciary in a matter uniquely within the ken of judges and rulemaking of this kind is akin to the Judiciary's traditional rulemaking. Judges may serve on the Commission without impairing the courts, and presidential appointment and for-cause removal of Commission members do not threaten judicial independence because the Commission is not a court. Judgment affirmed.
sections.Reasoning: Justice Blackmun restated the nondelegation test from J. W. Hampton: Congress may delegate as long as it lays down an intelligible principle to which the delegate must conform. The Court's jurisprudence has been driven by the practical understanding that in a complex society Congress cannot do its job without delegating power under broad general directives. Here Congress specified three goals of the guidelines, four purposes of sentencing, seven offense and eleven offender factors, the 25 percent range rule and many particular directives. That the Commission makes political and substantive choices does not matter; the delegations upheld in Yakus, Lichter and American Power & Light involved comparable discretion. On separation of powers, Blackmun described the Court's flexible approach, which asks whether an arrangement impermissibly aggrandizes one branch or undermines another. Congress has long given the courts rulemaking power over procedure and evidence under Sibbach and Hanna, and sentencing has always been a judicial function; the Commission's work is an appropriate exercise of that tradition even though the guidelines bind and have substantive effect. Judges' service on commissions has historical precedent, from Jay and Ellsworth to the Warren Commission, and the Commission's work does not require judges to act as prosecutors or to compromise impartiality in later cases. The President's appointment and for-cause removal power over Commission members does not touch judges' Article III tenure, since removal affects only Commission service.

topics.lrs-s-intelligible-principle: Scalia accepted the sufficiency of guidance under precedent while questioning judicial capacity to police degrees of discretion.
topics.lrs-s-accountability: The dispute concerned institutional placement, participation by judges, and whether rulemaking could stand apart from execution or adjudication.
topics.lrs-s-delegation-dimensions: Scalia's dissent argues the defect is the breadth of a freestanding lawmaking body, not the specificity of its instructions.
topics.lrs-s-removal: The Court upheld the President's good-cause removal power over Commission members, including the judicial members.

learning.separateOpinions: Eight to one. Justice Scalia dissented alone. He agreed that the statute stated an intelligible principle but argued that the Commission was a junior-varsity Congress, an independent body exercising pure lawmaking power unconnected to any executive or judicial function, and that the Constitution permits delegation of policy discretion only as an incident of the exercise of executive or judicial power.
